A peg is a small, solid object — usually shaped like a pin, spike, or knob — that is used to fasten, hold, hang, mark, or fix something in place. Think of it as a physical anchor point, or a fixed reference point. This core idea of "something that holds or fixes" runs through almost every meaning of the word.
1. A Pin or Spike That Holds Things Together or in Place

The most basic meaning of peg is a short, usually cylindrical piece of wood, metal, or plastic that is driven into a surface or fitted into a hole to hold things together or to keep something in position.

Examples of this type:

  • Tent peg: A pointed metal spike hammered into the ground to anchor the ropes and base of a tent. Without these, the tent would simply blow away.
  • Wooden peg in furniture: Traditional furniture (like old chairs or tables) was often joined together using wooden pegs fitted into holes, instead of screws or nails. These are sometimes called dowels.
  • Surveying peg: A peg or stake driven into the ground to mark the boundary of a piece of land or a point of reference on a construction site.

The key idea in all these: the peg goes into something and holds it firmly.
2. A Hook or Pin for Hanging Things

A peg can also be a hook or knob attached to a wall or board, used to hang objects on. You've almost certainly seen these.

  • A row of pegs near the entrance of a school or home, where children and guests hang their coats, bags, and hats.
  • "Hang your jacket on the peg by the door."

In this sense, the peg sticks out of a surface (rather than going into it), and things are draped or hung over it.
3. A Clothes Peg (Clothespin)

A clothes peg (called a clothespin in American English) is a small clip or clamp used to attach wet clothes to a washing line so they can dry.

There are two common types:

  • A simple forked piece of wood or plastic that you push over the fabric and line.
  • A spring-loaded clip that grips when you squeeze and releases when you let go.

"She hung the shirts on the line with clothes pegs."

In everyday Indian and British English, people often simply say "peg" when they mean a clothes peg.
4. A Tuning Peg on a Musical Instrument

On stringed instruments like the violin, guitar, sitar, or cello, the tuning pegs (also called machine heads on guitars) are the knobs at the top of the instrument's neck.

Each string is wound around a peg. When you turn the peg, it either tightens or loosens the string, which raises or lowers the note the string produces. This is how musicians tune their instruments.

So here, the peg still "holds" something (the string) but also gives you control over tension.
5. A Fixed Level or Rate — Especially in Finance

In economics and finance, a peg is a fixed, official rate at which one currency is tied to another (usually to a powerful currency like the US dollar). The idea is that the exchange rate doesn't float freely — it is held in place, just like a physical peg holds something.

  • "The Hong Kong dollar has a peg to the US dollar." This means the Hong Kong dollar is kept at a fixed rate against the dollar by the government.
  • If a country removes this fixed rate, it is said to have "broken the peg" or "abandoned the peg."

More broadly, a "peg" can refer to any fixed value or benchmark used as a reference point — a price ceiling, a target rate, a standard level. The image is the same: something is held steady, not allowed to drift.
6. A Measure of Alcohol (Especially Common in India and Britain)

In India and British English, a peg is a standard measure of a spirit, especially whisky. When you order or pour a peg of whisky, you're referring to a specific quantity.

  • In India, a small peg (often called a "small" or "chota peg") is typically 30 ml, and a large peg ("large" or "bada peg") is 60 ml.
  • "He poured himself a peg of whisky before dinner."
  • "Will you have a peg?"

This meaning is extremely common in everyday Indian English and very natural in social contexts.
7. A Score Marker in the Card Game Cribbage

In the traditional British card game Cribbage, players keep track of their scores using a special board called a cribbage board, which has rows of small holes. Players move small pin-like markers — called pegs — along these holes to show their running score.

This is a specialized use, but worth knowing: here, a peg is literally a small pin used as a marker.
8. A Wooden Leg (Old-Fashioned Informal)

In older literature and informal British speech, a peg (or "peg leg") could refer to a wooden prosthetic leg — the kind you associate with old-fashioned pirates in stories.

  • "Long John Silver had a peg for a leg."

This usage is largely historical and literary today, not common in modern everyday speech.
9. A Step or Degree (Used in the Phrase "Take Someone Down a Peg")

You may encounter the expression "take someone down a peg" (or "take them down a peg or two"). This is an idiom meaning to humble someone who is too arrogant or has too high an opinion of themselves — to reduce their pride or make them feel less important.

The image comes from old nautical practice: the "peg" represented a level or rank. To be "taken down a peg" literally meant to be lowered in rank or status.

  • "He was getting a bit too full of himself, so his boss took him down a peg in front of the team."

The Thread That Connects Everything

If you look across all these meanings, there is one underlying idea: a peg is something that fixes, anchors, or holds a position. Whether it is physically holding a tent to the ground, fixing a currency's value, marking a score, or holding a string at the right tension — the peg always serves as a point of stability and reference.

This is why the word is so versatile: the moment something is "pegged," it is held in place — whether literally or figuratively.
